title: Sophia's Garden Plot and Ravi's Newsletter
goal: I can add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators, write my answer in simplest form, and tell why an author wrote a piece.

card.desc: You help Sophia plan her garden plot: you find a common denominator, rename fractions as equivalent fractions, add and subtract them, write answers in simplest form (or as a mixed number), and compare fractions like 1/4 and 1/6. You start with a warm-up on Lessons 1 and 2. Then you read Ravi's Newsletter and decide whether each piece was written to inform, persuade or entertain (Pathways Week 8).

win: You made unlike fractions work together and figured out why every newsletter piece was written. Sophia's garden plot is planned!

slides.title: Sophia's Garden Plot and Ravi's Newsletter
slides.text: Sophia is planning a community garden plot. Tomatoes need 1/3 of it and peppers need 1/4. Those denominators do not match! Today you learn to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators. Then you read Ravi's neighborhood newsletter and figure out why each piece was written.

notes.do: Before class: check his Lesson 2 Show What You Know score (Formspree). Set out fraction strips: 1 whole bar, 2 halves, 3 thirds, 4 fourths, 6 sixths and 12 twelfths (28 pieces). Also three highlighters (three colors), whiteboard and marker, pencil and paper. Math runs 9:30–10:05 (35 min); reading runs 10:05–10:30 (25 min).
notes.say: Two jobs today. First 35 minutes: fractions that do not share a denominator. Last 25 minutes: a newsletter, and the reason behind every piece in it.
notes.ask: What do you remember about adding fractions like 1/5 + 2/5?
notes.listen: Add the numerators and keep the denominator: 3/5. If he adds the 5s too (3/10), note it: today's lesson fixes that.

slides.title: Sophia's plan
slides.text: Tomatoes need 1/3 of the plot. Peppers need 1/4.
prompts: Which needs more space, the tomatoes or the peppers? How do you know?
Do tomatoes and peppers together use more or less than half the plot? Make an estimate.
Why can't Sophia just add the tops and add the bottoms?
starters: You can't add the bottoms because …

notes.do: 2 to 3 minutes. Write his estimate (more or less than half) in the corner of the whiteboard. We check it at 9:46.
notes.ask: Which piece is bigger: one of 3 equal pieces, or one of 4 equal pieces?
notes.listen: 1/3 is bigger: fewer pieces means bigger pieces. For the estimate, any reasoned guess is fine; the exact answer (7/12) is a little more than half.

slides.title: Lessons 1 and 2, then fractions
slides.text: Paper first, then type.

items.q: Lesson 1 skill. Stack it: 53 × 24 = ____
items.no: Ones row: 53 × 4. Tens row: write the 0, then 53 × 2. Add.

items.q: Lesson 2 skill: 714 ÷ 6 = ____
items.no: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Write the check.

items.q: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. What is the first number on BOTH lists?
items.why: 12 is on both lists. It is the smallest number that both 3 and 4 divide into evenly.
items.no: Look for a number that is on both lists.
items.hint: It is the last number on each list.

items.q: Same denominators, like Pathways Week 3: 2/5 + 1/5 = ____
items.why: The pieces are the same size (fifths), so add the numerators: 2 + 1 = 3. Keep the denominator: 3/5.
items.no: Add the numerators. Keep the denominator.

notes.do: He answers out loud, writes on paper, then types. Circle the 12 on the whiteboard: it is today's common denominator.
notes.say: Adding fractions is easy when the pieces are the same size. Today we make the pieces the same size first.
notes.ask: Why is 2/5 + 1/5 not 3/10?
notes.listen: Fifths plus fifths are still fifths. The denominator names the size of the pieces; it does not get added.

slides.title: Math words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: The top number in a fraction. It counts the pieces you have.
words.example: In 3/4, the numerator is 3.

words.meaning: The bottom number in a fraction. It tells how many equal pieces make 1 whole.
words.example: In 3/4, the denominator is 4.

words.meaning: Fractions whose bottom numbers are different.
words.example: 1/3 and 1/4 have unlike denominators: 3 and 4.

words.meaning: A denominator that two or more fractions can share.
words.example: 12 is a common denominator for 1/3 and 1/4.

words.meaning: A fraction that names the same amount, written with different numbers.
words.example: 1/3 and 4/12 are equivalent fractions.

words.meaning: A smart, quick guess made by rounding first.
words.example: 1/3 and 1/4 are each less than 1/2, so my estimate is that 1/3 + 1/4 is less than 1.

words.meaning: A whole number and a fraction together.
words.example: 1 1/4 is a mixed number: 1 whole and 1/4 more.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud, then covers it and says the meaning in his own words.
notes.say: You will type these from memory at the end of class and all week. Pathways Week 8 asks you to TYPE common denominator, denominator and estimate.
notes.ask: Which number is the numerator in 3/4? What does the denominator tell you?
notes.listen: Numerator on top (3), denominator on the bottom (4): how many equal pieces make 1 whole. Have him spell denominator out loud (d-e-n-o-m-i-n-a-t-o-r).

steps.text: 4 twelfths cover the 1/3 strip exactly. So 1/3 = 4/12. Same length, same amount.
On paper: 3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 4 too: 1 × 4 = 4. 1/3 = 4/12.
Now the 1/4 strip: 3 twelfths cover it. 4 × 3 = 12 and 1 × 3 = 3, so 1/4 = 3/12.
1/3 and 4/12 are equivalent fractions. The pieces got smaller, so you need more of them. The amount did not change.

slides.tip: Multiply the numerator AND the denominator by the same number. Then the fraction keeps its value.

notes.do: Hands-on: he lays the whole bar, the 1/3 strip and the twelfths on the table and counts the twelfths that match. Then the 1/4 strip. He writes each equation on paper.
notes.say: Renaming a fraction is like trading one big piece for smaller pieces of the same total size.
notes.ask: Why do we multiply the top by 4 too, and not just the bottom?
notes.listen: If only the bottom changes, the pieces get smaller but you keep only 1 of them, so the amount shrinks. 1/12 is much less than 1/3.

slides.title: Rename the fractions
slides.text: Write each one on paper first. Use the strips if you want to check.

items.q: Rename it as an equivalent fraction. 3/4 = ____/12 Type the numerator.
items.why: 4 × 3 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 3 too: 3 × 3 = 9. 3/4 = 9/12.
items.no: What do you multiply 4 by to get 12? Multiply the numerator by the same number.

items.q: Rename it as an equivalent fraction. 2/3 = ____/12 Type the numerator.
items.why: 3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8. 2/3 = 8/12.
items.no: What do you multiply 3 by to get 12? Multiply the numerator by the same number.

items.q: Rename it as an equivalent fraction. 2/5 = ____/10 Type the numerator.
items.why: 5 × 2 = 10, so multiply the numerator by 2 too: 2 × 2 = 4. 2/5 = 4/10.
items.no: What do you multiply 5 by to get 10? Multiply the numerator by the same number.

notes.do: He checks 3/4 = 9/12 with the strips (3 fourths, 9 twelfths), then does the other two on paper only.
notes.ask: For 2/3 = ____/12, what did you multiply by? Why that number?
notes.listen: 3 × 4 = 12, so multiply by 4: 2 × 4 = 8. If he types 4 (the multiplier) instead of 8, ask: 4 what? Multiply the numerator by 4.

slides.title: Adding with unlike denominators: 1/3 + 1/4
slides.text: Back to Sophia's plot. The denominators 3 and 4 are unlike, so the pieces are different sizes.

steps.text: 1. Find a common denominator. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Use the first number on both lists: 12.
2. Rename. 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12 (from the strips).
3. Add or subtract the numerators. Keep the denominator. 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

steps.text: 4. Simplify. 7 and 12 can't both be divided by the same number, so 7/12 is already in simplest form.
Then check with an estimate. Half the plot is 6/12. 7/12 is a little more than 6/12, so tomatoes and peppers use a little more than half. Was your 9:30 estimate right?

slides.tip: Never add the denominators. 1/3 + 1/4 is NOT 2/7: 2/7 is even less than 1/3 by itself, and adding more can't make the amount smaller.

notes.do: He builds 4 twelfths + 3 twelfths with the strips and counts 7 twelfths. Then he lays them next to the 1/2 strip to see 7/12 is a little more than half.
notes.say: Four steps: common denominator, rename, add or subtract, simplify. Then check with an estimate.
notes.ask: Why is 2/7 impossible for 1/3 + 1/4?
notes.listen: The answer must be bigger than each part. 2/7 is smaller than 1/3, so it can't be right. Look back at his estimate from 9:30 and praise any reasoning.

slides.title: Add them
slides.text: Write the four steps on paper. Then type.

items.q: What is the smallest common denominator for 1/2 and 1/3?
items.why: Multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6. Multiples of 3: 3, 6. The first number on both lists is 6.
items.no: List the multiples of 2 and of 3.

items.q: 1/2 + 1/3 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6. Multiples of 3: 3, 6. The common denominator is 6. 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. 5/6
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 9 is a multiple of 3, so you only rename one fraction. 2/3 + 1/9 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: 9 is a multiple of 3, so the common denominator is 9. 2/3 = 6/9. 6/9 + 1/9 = 7/9. 7/9
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Only one fraction needs renaming: 9 is a multiple of 3, so 1/9 stays as it is and you rename 2/3. Then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

notes.do: He leads 1/2 + 1/3 with the strips (1 half = 3 sixths, 1 third = 2 sixths), then does 2/3 + 1/9 on paper only.
notes.ask: In 2/3 + 1/9, why don't you rename the 1/9?
notes.listen: 9 is already a multiple of 3, so 9 is the common denominator. Only 2/3 changes: 2/3 = 6/9. 6/9 + 1/9 = 7/9.

slides.title: Simplest form, and more than 1 whole
slides.text: Pathways wants every answer in simplest form: the smallest numbers that name the same amount.

visual.sub: divide the numerator and the denominator by 3

steps.text: Simplify. 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6. Both 3 and 6 can be divided by 3: 3/6 = 1/2.
Use the smallest common denominator. With 12 for 1/2 + 1/3 you get 6/12 + 4/12 = 10/12, and then you must simplify: 10/12 = 5/6. With 6 you get 5/6 right away.
More than 1 whole? Sophia wants beans on 1/2 of the plot too. 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/2 = 4/12 + 3/12 + 6/12 = 13/12.
12/12 is 1 whole, so 13/12 is 1 whole and 1/12 more: 13/12 = 1 1/12, a mixed number. That is MORE than the whole plot, so the beans do not fit!

slides.tip: Before you type, ask: can the numerator and denominator both be divided by the same number? Is the numerator bigger than the denominator?

notes.do: Strips: 1 sixth + 2 sixths = 3 sixths, laid next to the 1/2 strip. Then he stacks 4 twelfths + 3 twelfths + 6 twelfths: there are only 12 twelfths, so he runs out. That is why 13/12 is more than 1 whole.
notes.say: Pathways marks 10/12 wrong when it wants 5/6. Simplest form every time, unless the question says otherwise.
notes.ask: How do you know 13/12 is more than 1 whole?
notes.listen: The numerator (13) is bigger than the denominator (12). 12/12 = 1, plus 1/12 more.

slides.title: Simplify and use mixed numbers
slides.text: Paper first. Then type.

items.q: Simplify: 6/8 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Both 6 and 8 can be divided by 2: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. 6/8 = 3/4.
items.no: What number divides both 6 and 8?
items.hint: Divide the numerator and the denominator by 2.

items.q: 1/4 + 1/12 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: 12 is a multiple of 4, so the common denominator is 12. 1/4 = 3/12. 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12. Simplify: divide the numerator and the denominator by 4. 4/12 = 1/3. 1/3
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Only one fraction needs renaming: 12 is a multiple of 4, so 1/12 stays as it is and you rename 1/4. Then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 3/4 + 1/2 = ____ Type it as a mixed number in simplest form, like 1 1/2.
items.why: 4 is a multiple of 2, so the common denominator is 4. 1/2 = 2/4. 3/4 + 2/4 = 5/4. 5/4 is more than 1 whole (4/4 = 1): 5/4 = 1 1/4. 1 1/4
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Only one fraction needs renaming: 4 is a multiple of 2, so 3/4 stays as it is and you rename 1/2. Then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Simplify, and because the answer is more than 1 whole, type it as a mixed number (whole number, space, fraction), not as a fraction whose top number is bigger than its bottom number.

steps.text: How much MORE do tomatoes need than peppers? 1/3 − 1/4 = 4/12 − 3/12 = 1/12.
What's left for herbs? The whole plot is 1 = 12/12. Tomatoes and peppers use 7/12. 12/12 − 7/12 = 5/12.
Estimate with 1/2. Half the plot is 6/12. 5/12 is less than 6/12, so the herbs get less than half.
Which is bigger, 1/4 or 1/6? 1/4 = 3/12 and 1/6 = 2/12, so 1/4 is bigger. 6 is a bigger number than 4, but sixths are SMALLER pieces than fourths.

slides.tip: To compare, rename both with a common denominator. Then the bigger numerator wins.

notes.say: More pieces in the whole means smaller pieces. Do not let the bigger denominator fool you.

slides.title: Subtract and compare
slides.text: Paper first. Then type.

items.q: 1/2 − 1/5 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Multiples of 5: 5, 10. The common denominator is 10. 1/2 = 5/10 and 1/5 = 2/10. 5/10 − 2/10 = 3/10. 3/10
items.no: Did you subtract the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 1 − 3/8 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.no: Write 1 whole as 8/8 first, then subtract only the numerators and keep the 8. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: Which is bigger, 2/3 or 3/4? Type the bigger fraction.
items.why: Common denominator 12: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. 9/12 is more than 8/12, so 3/4 is bigger.
items.no: Rename both with a common denominator. Then compare the numerators.

notes.do: He writes each step. For 1 − 3/8 he writes 1 = 8/8 first.

slides.title: Be the checker
slides.text: Each one has a mistake. Find it.

items.q: Someone wrote: 1/4 + 2/3 = 3/7. What went wrong?
choices: They added the numerators AND the denominators. It is 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12.
Nothing. 3/7 is right.
They should have subtracted
3/7 is right but not in simplest form
items.why: Never add the denominators. 2/3 alone is more than 1/2, but 3/7 is less than 1/2, so 3/7 can't be right. 1/4 + 2/3 = 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12.
no: Estimate: 2/3 by itself is more than 1/2, but 3/7 is less than 1/2. Adding can't make it smaller.
The question is an addition. The mistake is HOW they added.
3/7 can't be simplified, and it is not the right amount anyway: it is less than 2/3.

items.q: Someone said: 1/6 is bigger than 1/4, because 6 is bigger than 4. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing. 1/6 is bigger.
They are equal, because both numerators are 1
Sixths are smaller pieces than fourths, so 1/4 is bigger: 3/12 is more than 2/12
You can't compare fractions with unlike denominators
items.why: More pieces in the whole means smaller pieces. 1/4 = 3/12 and 1/6 = 2/12, so 1/4 is bigger.
no: Look at the strips: the 1/6 piece is shorter than the 1/4 piece.
Same numerator does not mean same amount: one fourth and one sixth are different sizes.
You can: rename both as twelfths (3/12 and 2/12).

items.q: Someone wrote: 1/2 + 1/8 = 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8. What went wrong?
choices: They should have used 16 as the denominator
They changed the denominator of 1/2 but not the numerator. 1/2 = 4/8, so it is 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8.
Nothing. 2/8 is right.
2/8 is right, but it should be simplified to 1/4
items.why: 1/2 is not 1/8. When you multiply the denominator by 4, multiply the numerator by 4 too: 1/2 = 4/8. 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8.
no: 8 already works, because 8 is a multiple of 2. The mistake is in renaming 1/2.
2/8 is less than 1/2 by itself. Adding 1/8 has to make it MORE than 1/2.
Simplifying 2/8 does not help: 2/8 is the wrong amount. 1/2 was renamed wrong.

notes.do: He says which step went wrong for each one, and proves it with an estimate, the strips (fourths, sixths and twelfths are in the kit) or a quick drawing. The kit has no eighths, so for 1/2 + 1/8 he draws a bar cut into 8 parts and shades 4 of them.
notes.say: These are the three big fraction mistakes: adding the denominators, letting a big denominator fool you, and renaming only the bottom number.
notes.ask: How can an estimate catch the first and the last mistake?
notes.listen: In both, the answer is smaller than one of the parts, which can't happen when you add.

words.meaning: The reason a writer chose to write a piece: usually to inform, persuade, or entertain.
words.example: The author's purpose of a weather report is to inform.

words.meaning: To give facts or explain something clearly.
words.example: A weather report informs: rain on Tuesday, sunny on Wednesday.

words.meaning: To convince someone to think or act a certain way.
words.example: A toy ad tries to persuade you to buy the toy.

words.meaning: To amuse or interest the reader, often through humor or story.
words.example: A knock-knock joke is there to entertain you.

words.meaning: The perspective a writer sees a topic from: what the writer believes matters most.
words.example: A writer who wants a longer recess has the point of view that kids need time to play.

words.meaning: Specific facts or details that support a point.
words.example: “Recess is only 15 minutes long” is evidence for a longer recess.

slides.title: Why writers write
slides.text: Read both pieces out loud.

visual.text:
Why Writers Write
Every piece of writing has a purpose. A news article aims to INFORM you with facts. An ad or an opinion letter aims to PERSUADE you to think or act a certain way. A joke or story aims to ENTERTAIN you. Noticing the purpose helps you read more carefully — an ad written to sell something reads very differently than a report written to simply explain what happened.

Newsletter Notice: The Park Cleanup
“Join us Saturday at 9am for the annual Maple Street Park cleanup! Bring gloves if you have them — we'll supply trash bags and water. Last year, volunteers collected over 200 pounds of litter in just two hours.”

items.q: The park cleanup notice gives the day, the time and what to bring. Its purpose is to ________. Type one word.
items.why: It gives facts and details, so its purpose is to inform.
items.no: Does it give facts, try to convince you, or make you laugh?

items.q: How many pounds of litter did volunteers collect last year? Type the number.
items.why: The notice says volunteers collected “over 200 pounds of litter in just two hours.”
items.no: Look at the last sentence of the notice.

items.q: Why does knowing the purpose help you as a reader?
choices: It tells you how long the piece is
It helps you read more carefully
It means you can skip every ad
It proves every ad is false
items.why: The passage says: “Noticing the purpose helps you read more carefully.”
no: The purpose is about WHY it was written, not its length.
The passage never says to skip ads. It says an ad reads differently.
The passage never says ads are false.

slides.text: Read the crosswalk letter out loud.

visual.text:
Reader's Letter
“Our neighborhood REALLY needs a crosswalk near the elementary school. I've watched kids dash across that street every single morning, and cars don't always slow down. Please, everyone — sign the petition at the library and let's get this crosswalk built before someone gets hurt.”

items.q: What is the author's purpose of the crosswalk letter? Type one word.
items.why: The writer wants readers to act (sign the petition), so the purpose is to persuade.
items.no: Is the writer trying to get you to DO something?

items.q: Which detail is evidence the writer uses to support the letter?
choices: “Please, everyone — sign the petition”
“Join us Saturday at 9am”
“Our neighborhood REALLY needs a crosswalk”
“I've watched kids dash across that street every single morning, and cars don't always slow down”
items.why: It is a specific detail the writer saw: kids dashing across while cars don't always slow down. That supports the point.
no: That is what the writer asks you to DO, not a fact that supports the point.
That is from the park cleanup notice, not this letter.
That is the writer's opinion. Evidence is what backs it up.

items.q: Where can readers sign the petition? Type the place.
items.why: The letter says: “sign the petition at the library.”
items.no: Look at the last sentence.
items.hint: It is a building full of books.

slides.title: Purpose and point of view
slides.text: Purpose and point of view work together, but they are not the same thing.

visual.text: purpose = WHY · point of view = WHAT they believe

steps.text: Purpose = WHY the author wrote it. The crosswalk letter: to persuade.
Point of view = WHAT the writer believes matters most. The crosswalk letter: student safety should come first.
Clue words. Inform: facts, days, times, numbers. Persuade: please, should, needs, best, favorite. Entertain: jokes, riddles, funny stories.
Ravi's sections. Inform goes in News. Persuade goes in Opinions. Entertain goes in Fun & Games.
Two purposes at once. A piece can inform AND persuade. Then ask: what is its MAIN job?

words.meaning: The top number in a fraction. It counts the pieces you have.
words.example: In 3/4, the numerator is 3.

words.meaning: The bottom number in a fraction. It tells how many equal pieces make 1 whole.
words.example: In 3/4, the denominator is 4.

words.meaning: Fractions whose bottom numbers are different.
words.example: 1/3 and 1/4 have unlike denominators: 3 and 4.

words.meaning: A denominator that two or more fractions can share.
words.example: 12 is a common denominator for 1/3 and 1/4.

words.meaning: A fraction that names the same amount, written with different numbers.
words.example: 1/3 and 4/12 are equivalent fractions.

words.meaning: A smart, quick guess made by rounding first.
words.example: 1/3 and 1/4 are each less than 1/2, so my estimate is that 1/3 + 1/4 is less than 1.

words.meaning: A whole number and a fraction together.
words.example: 1 1/4 is a mixed number: 1 whole and 1/4 more.

words.meaning: The reason a writer chose to write a piece: usually to inform, persuade, or entertain.
words.example: The author's purpose of a weather report is to inform.

words.meaning: To give facts or explain something clearly.
words.example: A weather report informs: rain on Tuesday, sunny on Wednesday.

words.meaning: To convince someone to think or act a certain way.
words.example: A toy ad tries to persuade you to buy the toy.

words.meaning: To amuse or interest the reader, often through humor or story.
words.example: A knock-knock joke is there to entertain you.

words.meaning: The perspective a writer sees a topic from: what the writer believes matters most.
words.example: A writer who wants a longer recess has the point of view that kids need time to play.

words.meaning: Specific facts or details that support a point.
words.example: “Recess is only 15 minutes long” is evidence for a longer recess.

slides.title: Common denominator, rename, add, simplify

steps.text: 1. Common denominator. Multiples of 6: 6, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Use 12.
2. Rename. 1/6 = 2/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Multiply the numerator AND the denominator by the same number.
3. Add the numerators. 2/12 + 9/12 = 11/12. Keep the denominator.
4. Simplify. 11 and 12 can't both be divided by the same number, and 11/12 is less than 1 whole, so 11/12 is done.
Then check with an estimate. 3/4 by itself is more than 1/2, so the answer must be more than 1/2. 11/12 is. ✅

slides.tip: Simplest form every time. If the numerator is bigger than the denominator, write a mixed number.

slides.title: Rename and add
slides.text: Paper first. Then type.

items.q: Rename it as an equivalent fraction. 5/6 = ____/12 Type the numerator.
items.why: 6 × 2 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 2 too: 5 × 2 = 10. 5/6 = 10/12.
items.no: What do you multiply 6 by to get 12? Multiply the numerator by the same number.

items.q: 1/3 + 2/5 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15. The common denominator is 15. 1/3 = 5/15 and 2/5 = 6/15. 5/15 + 6/15 = 11/15. 11/15
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 3/8 + 1/2 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: 8 is a multiple of 2, so the common denominator is 8. 1/2 = 4/8. 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8. 7/8
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Only one fraction needs renaming: 8 is a multiple of 2, so 3/8 stays as it is and you rename 1/2. Then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

slides.title: Simplest form and mixed numbers
slides.text: Ask yourself: can I simplify? Is it more than 1 whole?

items.q: Simplify: 10/15 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Both 10 and 15 can be divided by 5: 10 ÷ 5 = 2 and 15 ÷ 5 = 3. 10/15 = 2/3.
items.no: What number divides both 10 and 15?
items.hint: Divide the numerator and the denominator by 5.

items.q: 1/10 + 2/5 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: 10 is a multiple of 5, so the common denominator is 10. 2/5 = 4/10. 1/10 + 4/10 = 5/10. Simplify: divide the numerator and the denominator by 5. 5/10 = 1/2. 1/2
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Only one fraction needs renaming: 10 is a multiple of 5, so 1/10 stays as it is and you rename 2/5. Then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 5/6 + 1/2 = ____ Type it as a mixed number in simplest form, like 1 1/2.
items.why: 6 is a multiple of 2, so the common denominator is 6. 1/2 = 3/6. 5/6 + 3/6 = 8/6. 8/6 is more than 1 whole (6/6 = 1): 8/6 = 1 2/6 = 1 1/3 (divide the 2 and the 6 by 2). 1 1/3
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Only one fraction needs renaming: 6 is a multiple of 2, so 5/6 stays as it is and you rename 1/2. Then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Simplify, and because the answer is more than 1 whole, type it as a mixed number (whole number, space, fraction), not as a fraction whose top number is bigger than its bottom number.

slides.title: Subtract, what's left, and compare
slides.text: Paper first. Then type.

items.q: 3/4 − 1/3 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. The common denominator is 12. 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/3 = 4/12. 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12. 5/12
items.no: Did you subtract the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: A garden plot is 1 whole. Beans use 2/5 of it. What fraction of the plot is left? 1 − 2/5 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.no: Write 1 whole as 5/5 first, then subtract only the numerators and keep the 5. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: Which is bigger, 3/8 or 1/3? Type the bigger fraction.
items.why: Common denominator 24: 3/8 = 9/24 and 1/3 = 8/24. 9/24 is more than 8/24, so 3/8 is bigger.
items.no: Rename both with a common denominator. Then compare the numerators.

teacher.objective: Math (35 min): Ethan finds a common denominator for fractions with unlike denominators, renames fractions as equivalent fractions (multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the same number), adds and subtracts them, writes every answer in simplest form, writes a sum greater than 1 whole as a mixed number, compares unlike fractions, and checks with an estimate using 1/2 and 1. Reading (25 min): he identifies the author's purpose (inform, persuade, entertain) of each piece in Ravi's Newsletter, tells purpose from point of view, finds evidence in the crosswalk letter, explains how the bakery spotlight blends two purposes, sorts pieces into News, Opinions and Fun & Games, and types the math and reading words from memory.
materials: The class lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)

Fraction strips: 1 whole bar, 2 halves, 3 thirds, 4 fourths, 6 sixths and 12 twelfths (28 pieces; a printed fraction-strip chart cut apart works). The most used at one time is 7 twelfths (slide 7) and all 12 twelfths (slide 9, where he runs out on purpose).
Three highlighters or colored pencils (color 1 = inform, color 2 = persuade, color 3 = entertain)
Whiteboard and marker (his estimate at 9:30; PURPOSE = WHY and POINT OF VIEW = WHAT at 10:16)
Pencil and paper; Packet (2 pages), printed: page 1 Saturday, page 2 Sunday

plan.do: Class slides 1–2. He estimates whether 1/3 + 1/4 is more or less than half. Write his estimate in the corner of the whiteboard.
Class slide 3. 53 × 24 (Lesson 1) and 714 ÷ 6 (Lesson 2) as spaced review, then the first number on the multiples lists of 3 and 4, and 2/5 + 1/5.
Class slide 4. Numerator, denominator, unlike denominators, common denominator, equivalent fraction, estimate, mixed number. He spells denominator out loud.
Class slide 5. Fraction strips: 4 twelfths cover 1/3, 3 twelfths cover 1/4. He writes 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12.

Class slides 7–8. 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12 with the four steps (common denominator, rename, add or subtract, simplify, then check with an estimate); compare to his 9:30 estimate. Then he leads 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 and 2/3 + 1/9 = 7/9.
Class slides 11–12. 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12; herbs get 12/12 − 7/12 = 5/12, less than half; 1/4 is bigger than 1/6. Then 1/2 − 1/5, 1 − 3/8, and 2/3 vs 3/4.

Class slide 13. Added the denominators, the bigger-denominator trap, and renaming only the bottom number. He proves each with an estimate, the strips or a quick drawing (the kit has no eighths, so he draws those).
Class slide 14 on his own: 3/5 + 1/4 and 5/6 − 1/3. Note his first answers.
Class slide 15. Author's purpose, inform, persuade, entertain, point of view, evidence. Extra time on persuade and point of view.

plan.block: 10:08 · Why writers write + the park cleanup
plan.do: Class slide 16. He reads aloud and highlights the facts in the cleanup notice in color 1.
Class slide 17. Persuasive words in color 2, evidence in color 1. What does the writer want readers to DO?
Class slide 18. Write PURPOSE = WHY and POINT OF VIEW = WHAT on the whiteboard; he gives one example of each from the crosswalk letter.

plan.block: 10:19 · The joke and the bakery spotlight
plan.do: Class slide 19. The joke in color 3. In the bakery spotlight he marks facts (color 1) and persuasion (color 2): two purposes, main purpose persuade.
Class slide 20. He sorts six pieces into News, Opinions and Fun & Games and says the purpose before each tap.
Class slide 21. Denominator, purpose, persuade typed with no peeking.
Class slide 22. He says the steps for 1/3 + 1/4. Open the course page and read this week's task list.

watch: Adding the denominators: writing 2/7 as the answer to 1/3 + 1/4 is the big one. Catch it with an estimate: the answer must be bigger than each part, and 2/7 is less than 1/3.

Renaming only the bottom: 1/2 + 1/8 written as 1/8 + 1/8. Whatever he multiplies the denominator by, he multiplies the numerator by too. On renaming items, watch for him typing the multiplier (4) instead of the new numerator (8).

Simplest form: Pathways Week 8 marks most answers right ONLY in simplest form (it wants 5/6, not 10/12, and 3/4, not 6/8). It accepts 3/12 or 1/4 and 9/12 or 3/4 on the two crisis questions only. Using the SMALLEST common denominator saves a simplifying step. He checks: can the numerator and denominator both be divided by the same number?

More than 1 whole: if the numerator is bigger than the denominator, the answer is more than 1 whole. Our questions say when they want a mixed number (type it like 1 1/2). Pathways Week 8 itself has no answers over 1, but its paper challenge (design your own plot with three fractions) can go over 1.
The bigger-denominator trap: “6 is bigger than 4, so 1/6 is bigger.” Pathways has this exact wrong choice. More pieces means smaller pieces; prove it with the strips or with twelfths (3/12 vs 2/12).
Typing fractions: he types 5/6 with a slash, no spaces needed. He has lost points on typed answers that were right on paper, so he compares the typed answer to his paper before pressing Check.
Purpose vs point of view: purpose is WHY (inform, persuade, entertain); point of view is WHAT the writer believes. The bakery spotlight both informs and persuades; its MAIN purpose is persuade.

Pathways Week 8 Reading typed answers: it accepts inform, persuade, evidence and author's purpose as typed. On the Boss question “in a few words, what is this whole lesson really about?” it only accepts one exact word or phrase: purpose, inform, entertain or point of view (on the first question set it does NOT accept “persuade” or “author's purpose”). Tell him to type purpose there.

Curly apostrophe on the iPad: Pathways Week 8 Reading only accepts “author's purpose” typed with a straight apostrophe ('). iPad autocorrect turns it into a curly one (’) and the answer is marked wrong. Have him type just purpose where that works, or turn off Smart Punctuation (Settings, General, Keyboard) before he starts.

Inform: the hours (Saturdays 8am-2pm) or the address (214 Maple Street). Persuade: “Try their cinnamon rolls, voted a neighborhood favorite three years running.” Main purpose: persuade.
Any sentence that tries to get neighbors to come, using please or should. Example: Please come to the park cleanup on Saturday, because our park should be clean for everyone.

teacher.notes: For you only (do not share with Ethan): reading is a strength (98 on the first try on Pathways Week 6 Reading, and every story question right on the Unit 1 checkpoint), so the reading block is shorter and pushes for purpose vs point of view and the typed vocabulary Pathways asks for. His facts are strong, which helps with multiples lists and renaming. He is weaker on long multi-step procedures and on TYPED answers compared with multiple choice, so this lesson is mostly typed answers and every fraction problem uses the same four steps. Four steps: common denominator, rename, add or subtract, simplify. Then check with an estimate. Writing vocabulary words from memory is weak, so every part ends with words typed from memory. Before class, check his Lesson 2 Show What You Know score: if it is under 85, spend the first 2 minutes of the warm-up on one more long division problem with the check written. Finish: if both math exit-ticket problems are right on the first try, in simplest form, he is ready for Pathways Week 8 Math (Tuesday on his task list, aim for 85). Pathways Week 8 Reading is on Thursday of his task list; he already read all four newsletter pieces in class. The after-class lesson and Practice also use four KCE extra pieces for Ravi's newsletter (Library News, Riddle Corner, Fix the Fountain and Dog Wash; not in the Pathways lesson), labeled “More from Ravi's newsletter” on his screen. Both Pathways lessons stop for a paper Pre-Lesson Warm-Up and a Post-Lesson Challenge; print them from the Pathways pre/post page if you want him to do the pencil breaks on paper. Tonight he does the after-class lesson (about 25 to 30 minutes, including Show What You Know); it ends with Show What You Know (10 questions: 6 math and 4 reading; 3 different sets for retakes; he needs 85). If he scores under 85, look at the Formspree missed list: a missed rename or add means 10 minutes with the strips and the four steps at the start of next lesson; an answer that was right but not simplified means a simplest-form drill (6/8, 10/12, 9/12); a missed purpose question means sorting three short pieces out loud; a missed word means index-card practice.
